claim: Association between hearing impairment and dementia has been widely documented by epidemiological studies.
source: Although association between hearing impairment and dementia has been widely documented by epidemiological studies, the role of auditory sensory deprivation in cognitive decline remains to be fully understood.
evidence: The claim references epidemiological studies that have documented this association, indicating citation-based support.

claim: Hearing loss induced by noise exposure in 3×Tg-AD mice before phenotype manifestation caused persistent synaptic and morphological alterations in the auditory cortex.
source: We found that hearing loss induced by noise exposure in the 3×Tg-AD mice before the phenotype is manifested caused persistent synaptic and morphological alterations in the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by electrophysiological and morphological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hearing loss in 3×Tg-AD mice was associated with earlier hippocampal dysfunction compared to not-exposed animals.
source: This was associated with earlier hippocampal dysfunction, increased tau phosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and redox imbalance, along with anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of the neurodegenerative phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing hippocampal functional changes in noise-exposed AD mice.

claim: Hearing loss in 3×Tg-AD mice was associated with increased tau phosphorylation.
source: This was associated with earlier hippocampal dysfunction, increased tau phosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and redox imbalance, along with anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of the neurodegenerative phenotype.
evidence: Western blot data in the manuscript demonstrate increased tau phosphorylation in noise-exposed AD mice.

claim: Hearing loss in 3×Tg-AD mice was associated with neuroinflammation.
source: This was associated with earlier hippocampal dysfunction, increased tau phosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and redox imbalance, along with anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of the neurodegenerative phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on inflammatory markers (TNF-α, IL-1β) showing increased neuroinflammation.

claim: Hearing loss in 3×Tg-AD mice was associated with redox imbalance.
source: This was associated with earlier hippocampal dysfunction, increased tau phosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and redox imbalance, along with anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of the neurodegenerative phenotype.
evidence: Oxidative stress markers (ROS, 4-HNE, nitrotyrosine) were measured and showed increased levels in noise-exposed AD mice.

claim: Hearing loss in 3×Tg-AD mice was associated with anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of the neurodegenerative phenotype.
source: This was associated with earlier hippocampal dysfunction, increased tau phosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and redox imbalance, along with anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of the neurodegenerative phenotype.
evidence: Behavioral testing (NOR test) showed memory deficits at 6 months in noise-exposed AD mice, earlier than expected.

claim: A mouse model of AD is more vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss.
source: Our data suggest that a mouse model of AD is more vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss and shows reduced ability to counteract noise-induced detrimental effects, which accelerates the neurodegenerative disease onset.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing persistent alterations in AD mice but recovery in WT mice.

claim: A mouse model of AD shows reduced ability to counteract noise-induced detrimental effects.
source: Our data suggest that a mouse model of AD is more vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss and shows reduced ability to counteract noise-induced detrimental effects, which accelerates the neurodegenerative disease onset.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of recovery in AD mice and the absence of HO-1 upregulation compared to WT mice.

claim: Hearing loss accelerates neurodegenerative disease onset in a mouse model of AD.
source: Our data suggest that a mouse model of AD is more vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss and shows reduced ability to counteract noise-induced detrimental effects, which accelerates the neurodegenerative disease onset.
evidence: This is supported by the earlier appearance of memory deficits and pathological markers in noise-exposed AD mice.

claim: Impairments in peripheral and central auditory structures have been linked to incidence and acceleration of cognitive deficits.
source: Specifically, impairments in peripheral and central auditory structures have been linked to incidence and acceleration of cognitive deficits (Bernabei et al., 2014; Amieva et al., 2015; Fortunato et al., 2016; Deal et al., 2017) as well as to increased risk for the onset of neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Gates et al., 2002; Panza et al., 2015; Taljaard et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: Impairments in peripheral and central auditory structures have been linked to increased risk for the onset of neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease.
source: Specifically, impairments in peripheral and central auditory structures have been linked to incidence and acceleration of cognitive deficits (Bernabei et al., 2014; Amieva et al., 2015; Fortunato et al., 2016; Deal et al., 2017) as well as to increased risk for the onset of neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Gates et al., 2002; Panza et al., 2015; Taljaard et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: For every 10 dB increase in hearing loss, there is a 20% increased risk of developing dementia.
source: Accordingly, it has been shown that for every 10 dB increase in hearing loss, there is a 20% increased risk of developing dementia (Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2011.

claim: Hearing loss can be considered as a modifiable risk factor for dementia.
source: Indeed, while it is difficult to counteract neurodegeneration, hearing loss can be considered as a modifiable risk factor, given that it could be widely treated with hearing aids or cochlear implants.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge that hearing loss can be treated with hearing aids or cochlear implants.

claim: Hearing loss causes a cascade of changes in the main auditory pathway and in non-lemniscal brain regions, such as the hippocampus.
source: It has been reported that hearing loss causes a cascade of changes in the main auditory pathway and in non-lemniscal brain regions, such as the hippocampus (Manikandan et al., 2006; Goble et al., 2009; Cui et al., 2018; Nadhimi and Llano, 2021), a brain structure involved in memory and severely impaired in cognitive decline and AD.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The hippocampus is a brain structure involved in memory and severely impaired in cognitive decline and AD.
source: It has been reported that hearing loss causes a cascade of changes in the main auditory pathway and in non-lemniscal brain regions, such as the hippocampus (Manikandan et al., 2006; Goble et al., 2009; Cui et al., 2018; Nadhimi and Llano, 2021), a brain structure involved in memory and severely impaired in cognitive decline and AD.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the hippocampus.

claim: Sensory disruption due to damage of the organ of Corti may trigger central mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity.
source: Sensory disruption due to damage of the organ of Corti may trigger central mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity (Rauschecker, 1999; Syka, 2002; Caspary et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011) and changes in excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory networks along the central auditory pathway have been described (Liberman and Kiang, 1978; Abbott et al., 1999; Milbrandt et al., 2000; Salvi et al., 2000; Richardson et al., 2012; Engineer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory networks along the central auditory pathway have been described following sensory disruption.
source: Sensory disruption due to damage of the organ of Corti may trigger central mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity (Rauschecker, 1999; Syka, 2002; Caspary et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011) and changes in excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory networks along the central auditory pathway have been described (Liberman and Kiang, 1978; Abbott et al., 1999; Milbrandt et al., 2000; Salvi et al., 2000; Richardson et al., 2012; Engineer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Exposure to loud sounds led to structural plasticity changes in central auditory structures, resulting in decreased spine density and altered dendritic complexity in pyramidal neurons of layer II/III of the auditory cortex.
source: In previous studies we showed that exposure to loud sounds led to structural plasticity changes in central auditory structures, resulting in decreased spine density and altered dendritic complexity in pyramidal neurons of layer II/III of the auditory cortex (ACx) (Fetoni et al., 2013; Fetoni et al., 2015; Paciello et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim refers to the authors' previous published studies.

claim: Neurons in the hippocampus respond to acoustic stimuli.
source: It is also known that neurons in the hippocampus respond to acoustic stimuli (Moita et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2018); indeed, auditory potentials can be evoked in this structure (Bickford-Wimer et al., 1990; Moxon et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Auditory potentials can be evoked in the hippocampus.
source: It is also known that neurons in the hippocampus respond to acoustic stimuli (Moita et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2018); indeed, auditory potentials can be evoked in this structure (Bickford-Wimer et al., 1990; Moxon et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hearing loss can affect hippocampal functions by altering neurotransmitter levels.
source: Moreover, data from animal models suggest that hearing loss can affect hippocampal functions by altering neurotransmitter levels (Cui et al., 2009; Chengzhi et al., 2011; Cui and Li, 2013; Beckmann et al., 2020) and by decreasing neurogenesis (Tao et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Kurioka et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous animal model studies.

claim: Hearing loss can affect hippocampal functions by decreasing neurogenesis.
source: Moreover, data from animal models suggest that hearing loss can affect hippocampal functions by altering neurotransmitter levels (Cui et al., 2009; Chengzhi et al., 2011; Cui and Li, 2013; Beckmann et al., 2020) and by decreasing neurogenesis (Tao et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Kurioka et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous animal model studies.

claim: No studies have yet characterized the impact of auditory sensory deprivation on the onset and time-course of cognitive decline in AD and the underlying mechanisms.
source: However, to our knowledge, no studies have yet characterized the impact of auditory sensory deprivation on the onset and time-course of cognitive decline in AD and the underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: 3×Tg AD mice are a common experimental model of AD.
source: To this aim, we used 3×Tg AD mice, a common experimental model of AD, which experienced hearing loss induced by noise exposure at an age of 2 months, when the AD phenotype is not manifested yet.
evidence: This is established knowledge about this mouse model in AD research.

claim: At 2 months of age, the AD phenotype is not manifested yet in 3×Tg AD mice.
source: To this aim, we used 3×Tg AD mice, a common experimental model of AD, which experienced hearing loss induced by noise exposure at an age of 2 months, when the AD phenotype is not manifested yet.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the timeline of phenotype development in this mouse model.

claim: Baseline mean ABR thresholds ranged from 40 to 20 dB SPL across frequencies in 3×Tg-AD and WT mice.
source: Baseline mean ABR thresholds ranged from 40 to 20 dB sound pressure level (SPL) across frequencies, with no significant differences between 3×Tg-AD and WT mice (Figure 2A; AD-NN n = 12; WT-NN n = 11; three-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, p = 0.80).
evidence: This is supported by ABR measurements presented in the study and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There were no significant differences in baseline ABR thresholds between 3×Tg-AD and WT mice.
source: Baseline mean ABR thresholds ranged from 40 to 20 dB sound pressure level (SPL) across frequencies, with no significant differences between 3×Tg-AD and WT mice (Figure 2A; AD-NN n = 12; WT-NN n = 11; three-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, p = 0.80).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ABR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Repeated noise exposure worsened threshold pattern, reaching a threshold increased value of about 40 dB 1 month after noise exposure.
source: In line with our previous reports (Fetoni et al., 2013; Paciello et al., 2018), repeated noise exposure worsened threshold pattern, reaching a threshold increased value of about 40 dB 1 month after noise exposure (3 M, Figure 2A and C; WT-NE n = 8, AD-NE n = 7; three-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, WT-NE vs. WT-NN, p = 0.0001; AD-NE vs. AD-NN, p = 0.0002).
evidence: This is supported by ABR measurements and statistical analysis, consistent with previous studies.

claim: The trend of threshold increase was similar across mid- and high frequencies in both 3×Tg-AD and WT mice.
source: The trend of threshold increase was similar across mid- and high frequencies and no significant differences were observed between 3×Tg-AD and WT mice, indicating that both strains show a similar degree of susceptibility to hearing loss induced by noise.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ABR data across different frequencies.

claim: Both 3×Tg-AD and WT strains show a similar degree of susceptibility to hearing loss induced by noise.
source: The trend of threshold increase was similar across mid- and high frequencies and no significant differences were observed between 3×Tg-AD and WT mice, indicating that both strains show a similar degree of susceptibility to hearing loss induced by noise.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ABR data showing similar threshold increases in both strains.

claim: At 6 M, both WT-NN and AD-NN showed a slight increase (about 20 dB) in auditory threshold values compared to younger mice.
source: At 6 M, both WT-NN and AD-NN showed a slight increase (about 20 dB) in auditory threshold values (Figure 2B) compared to younger mice, probably as a consequence of physiological age-related worsening of cochlear function.
evidence: This is based on ABR measurements at different time points shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The slight increase in auditory threshold values at 6 M in WT-NN and AD-NN mice is probably a consequence of physiological age-related worsening of cochlear function.
source: At 6 M, both WT-NN and AD-NN showed a slight increase (about 20 dB) in auditory threshold values (Figure 2B) compared to younger mice, probably as a consequence of physiological age-related worsening of cochlear function.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed threshold increase.

claim: When comparing noise-exposed 6 M animals with age-matched not-exposed animals, a significant increase in auditory threshold was observed, specifically in the range of mid-frequencies.
source: Of note, when comparing noise-exposed 6 M animals with age-matched not-exposed animals, a significant increase in auditory threshold was observed, specifically in the range of mid-frequencies, indicating that noise can induce a permanent hearing loss over time (Figure 2B; WT-NN n = 9, AD-NN n = 13; WT-NE n = 7, AD-NE n = 11; three-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, WT-NN vs. WT-NE, p = 0.017; AD-NN vs. AD-NE, p = 0.003).
evidence: This is supported by ABR measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Noise can induce a permanent hearing loss over time.
source: Of note, when comparing noise-exposed 6 M animals with age-matched not-exposed animals, a significant increase in auditory threshold was observed, specifically in the range of mid-frequencies, indicating that noise can induce a permanent hearing loss over time (Figure 2B; WT-NN n = 9, AD-NN n = 13; WT-NE n = 7, AD-NE n = 11; three-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, WT-NN vs. WT-NE, p = 0.017; AD-NN vs. AD-NE, p = 0.003).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the persistent threshold elevation observed at 6 M.

claim: An auditory threshold worsening of about 20–25 dB was still detectable in noise-exposed mice at 6 M, compared to age-matched not-exposed animals, in both 3×Tg-AD and WT mice with no significant differences between strains.
source: In fact, an auditory threshold worsening of about 20–25 dB was still detectable in noise-exposed mice, compared to age-matched not-exposed animals, in both 3×Tg-AD and WT mice with no significant differences between strains.
evidence: This is based on ABR measurements at 6 M comparing exposed and not-exposed animals.

claim: Noise exposure significantly increased latency of ABR Waves I and II at different intensities in both WT and 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: Analysis of latency-intensity curves showed that noise exposure significantly increased latency of ABR Waves I and II at different intensities (Figure 2C–D; WT- NN n = 8, AD-NN n = 10; WT-NE n = 7, AD-NE n = 7; Student's t-test) in both WT and 3×Tg-AD mice.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of ABR latency data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: Increased latency of ABR Waves I and II suggests that noise exposure induced an impairment of the number of neural unit firing.
source: These findings suggest that noise exposure induced an impairment of the number of neural unit firing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the increased ABR latency data.

claim: Noise exposure can induce a hearing loss that persists over time and similarly affects cochlear function in both 3×Tg-AD and WT mice.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that noise exposure can induce a hearing loss that persists over time and similarly affects cochlear function in both 3×Tg-AD and WT mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ABR data presented.

claim: 1 month after the onset of trauma sessions, fEPSPs were significantly smaller in animals subjected to noise compared to those not exposed in WT mice.
source: As expected on the basis of our previous findings (Paciello et al., 2018), 1 month after the onset of trauma sessions, comparison of the input/output (I/O) curves, obtained by plotting EPSP amplitude against stimulus intensities, showed that fEPSPs were significantly smaller in animals subjected to noise compared to those not exposed, with similar results in WT (Figure 3A; n = 17 slices from three WT-NE and n = 11 slices from five WT-NN; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,126) = 59.5, p < 0.001) and 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 3B; n = 13 slices from five AD-NE and n = 15 slices from six AD-NN; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,126) = 15.302, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3A and consistent with previous findings.

claim: 1 month after the onset of trauma sessions, fEPSPs were significantly smaller in animals subjected to noise compared to those not exposed in 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: As expected on the basis of our previous findings (Paciello et al., 2018), 1 month after the onset of trauma sessions, comparison of the input/output (I/O) curves, obtained by plotting EPSP amplitude against stimulus intensities, showed that fEPSPs were significantly smaller in animals subjected to noise compared to those not exposed, with similar results in WT (Figure 3A; n = 17 slices from three WT-NE and n = 11 slices from five WT-NN; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,126) = 59.5, p < 0.001) and 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 3B; n = 13 slices from five AD-NE and n = 15 slices from six AD-NN; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,126) = 15.302, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B and consistent with previous findings.

claim: At 6 M, no significant differences in fEPSP amplitude were observed between WT-NN and WT-NE animals in the auditory cortex.
source: Interestingly, at 6 M, no significant differences between WT-NN and WT-NE animals (Figure 3C; n = 20 slices from eight WT-NE and n = 21 slices from seven WT-NN mice; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,117) = 0.084, p = 0.773) were observed.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At 6 M, decreased fEPSP response (of about 30%) was found in AD-NE compared to age-matched not-exposed animals in the auditory cortex.
source: Conversely, at 6 M, decreased response (of about 30%) was found in AD-NE compared to age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; n = 14 slices from five AD-NE and n = 12 slices from five AD-NN mice; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,72) = 12.53, p < 0.001), suggesting that in this mouse strain auditory cortex was most severely affected by noise.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In 3×Tg-AD mice, auditory cortex was most severely affected by noise compared to WT mice.
source: Conversely, at 6 M, decreased response (of about 30%) was found in AD-NE compared to age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; n = 14 slices from five AD-NE and n = 12 slices from five AD-NN mice; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,72) = 12.53, p < 0.001), suggesting that in this mouse strain auditory cortex was most severely affected by noise.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential recovery between WT and AD mice.

claim: Phosphorylation of AMPA receptor GluA1 subunit at Ser845 plays a role in AMPAR function, trafficking, and channel conductance.
source: To further assess the effect of hearing loss on glutamatergic transmission, phosphorylation of AMPA receptor (AMPAR) GluA1 subunit at Ser845 (pGluA1Ser845) was also evaluated in our experimental conditions because of its role in AMPAR function, trafficking, and channel conductance (Derkach et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2000; Suzuki et al., 2005; Havekes et al., 2007; Man et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hearing loss significantly decreased the levels of pGluA1Ser845 (by approximately 60%) in ACx of 6 M AD-NE mice compared to age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: Although no difference in pGluA1Ser845 expression was found in ACx of of 3 M animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), our Western immunoblot analyses performed on ACx extracts from 6 M 3×Tg -AD and WT mice revealed that hearing loss significantly decreased the levels of pGluA1Ser845 (by approximately 60%) in AD-NE mice (Figure 3E; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN, p = 0.0001), compared to age-matched not-exposed animals.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 1 month after noise exposure, the number of spines in apical and basal dendrites in both WT and 3×Tg AD animals was significantly reduced.
source: Consistent with our previous studies (Fetoni et al., 2015; Paciello et al., 2018), 1 month after noise exposure, the number of spines in apical and basal dendrites in both WT and 3× Tg AD animals was significantly reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by spine density analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and consistent with previous studies.

claim: At 6 M, spine density in both apical and basal dendrites in neurons of ACx layer II/III was decreased in AD-NE mice compared with age-matched AD-NN animals.
source: In line with functional evaluations, analysis at the subsequent time point (i.e., 4 months after noise exposure) showed a decreased spine density in both apical and basal dendrites in neurons of 6 M AD-NE mice compared with age-matched AD-NN animals (Figure 4B and D; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,142) = 6.94, apical dendrites, n = 36 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 38 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.011; basal dendrites, n = 32 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 32 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.012).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figures 4B and D.

claim: At 6 M, no significant differences in spine number were observed when comparing WT-NE and WT-NN groups in ACx layer II/III.
source: No significant differences in spine number were, instead, observed when comparing WT-NE and groups (Figure 4A and C; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, p = 0.88; n = 40 neurons from four WT-NN animals, n = 30 neurons from four WT-NE animals; basal dendrites, p = 0.70; n = 30 neurons from four WT-NN animals, n = 30 neurons from four WT-NE animals).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figures 4A and C.

claim: Western blot analysis showed significantly lower levels of PSD-95 in ACx of 6 M 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise compared with their age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: In keeping with these data, Western blot analysis showed significantly lower levels of PSD-95 in ACx of 3×Tg-AD mice and not in WT exposed to noise compared with their respective age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 4E and F; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice p = 0.025).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 4E and F.

claim: 3×Tg-AD mice are most vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss as they cannot recover over time functional and morphological alterations induced by sensory deprivation in the ACx.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that 3×Tg-AD mice are most vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss as they cannot recover over time functional and morphological alterations induced by sensory deprivation in the ACx.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the functional and morphological data in ACx.

claim: Cortical and cognitive adaptation to the loss of a sensory modality impacts on information processing ability of cortical structures.
source: Indeed, several evidences suggest that cortical and cognitive adaptation to the loss of a sensory modality impacts on information processing ability of cortical structures, and this, in turn, compromises the ability of the hippocampus to reliably and effectively encode and store sensory experience (Feldmann et al., 2019; Beckmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of a sensory modality compromises the ability of the hippocampus to reliably and effectively encode and store sensory experience.
source: Indeed, several evidences suggest that cortical and cognitive adaptation to the loss of a sensory modality impacts on information processing ability of cortical structures, and this, in turn, compromises the ability of the hippocampus to reliably and effectively encode and store sensory experience (Feldmann et al., 2019; Beckmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Noise affected basal synaptic transmission only in AD mice at 6 M in the hippocampus.
source: As shown in Figure 5, noise affected basal synaptic transmission only in AD mice. In fact, fEPSP amplitudes were significantly reduced in AD-NE mice with respect to age-matched AD-NN animals (Figure 5B; n = 11 slices from four AD-NE mice and n = 12 slices from four AD-NN mice; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,126), p = 0.020).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in hippocampus shown in Figure 5B.

claim: fEPSP amplitudes in hippocampal CA1 were significantly reduced in 6 M AD-NE mice with respect to age-matched AD-NN animals.
source: As shown in Figure 5, noise affected basal synaptic transmission only in AD mice. In fact, fEPSP amplitudes were significantly reduced in AD-NE mice with respect to age-matched AD-NN animals (Figure 5B; n = 11 slices from four AD-NE mice and n = 12 slices from four AD-NN mice; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,126), p = 0.020).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No significant differences in hippocampal fEPSP amplitudes were observed between noise-exposed and non-exposed animals of WT strain at 6 M.
source: On the other hand, no significant differences were observed between noise-exposed and non-exposed animals of WT strain (Figure 5A; n = 12 slices from six WT-NE mice and n = 14 slices from seven WT-NN mice; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,120), p = 0.78).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A significant decrease of spine density was observed in CA1 and DG of the hippocampus in 6 M AD-NE mice compared with age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: In line with functional data, morphological analyses showed a significant decrease of spine density in CA1 and dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus in AD-NE mice.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data presented in Figure 6.

claim: A decreased number of dendritic spines were observed in apical and basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons in 6 M AD-NE mice compared with age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: As shown in Figure 6, a decreased number of dendritic spines were observed in transgenic mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals, both in apical and basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons (Figure 6B and D; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,63) = 41.66, apical dendrites, n = 35 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 30 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.0001; basal dendrites, n = 37 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 34 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.0009) and in dendrites of DG granular cells (Figure 6F and H; one-way ANOVA, F(1,63) = 11.51, n = 31 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 34 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figures 6B and D.

claim: A decreased number of dendritic spines were observed in dendrites of DG granular cells in 6 M AD-NE mice compared with age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: As shown in Figure 6, a decreased number of dendritic spines were observed in transgenic mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals, both in apical and basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons (Figure 6B and D; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,63) = 41.66, apical dendrites, n = 35 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 30 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.0001; basal dendrites, n = 37 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 34 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.0009) and in dendrites of DG granular cells (Figure 6F and H; one-way ANOVA, F(1,63) = 11.51, n = 31 neurons from four AD-NN animals, n = 34 neurons from four AD-NE animals, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figures 6F and H.

claim: No significant differences in hippocampal spine density were observed between noise-exposed and not-exposed mice in the WT group at 6 M.
source: No significant differences were observed between noise-exposed and not-exposed mice in the WT group (Figure 6A, C, E and G; CA1, two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test, F(1,59) = 0.21, p = 0.64, apical dendrites, n = 41 neurons from four WT-NN animals, n = 30 neurons from four WT-NE animals; basal dendrites, n = 31 neurons from four WT-NN animals, n = 31 neurons from four WT-NE animals; DG, one-way ANOVA F(1,78) = 0.16, p = 0.68, n = 44 neurons from four WT-NN animals, n = 36 neurons from four WT-NE animals).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figures 6A, C, E, and G.

claim: Western blot analysis showed a significantly lower expression of PSD-95 in hippocampus of 6 M 3×Tg-AD animals exposed to noise compared with not-exposed animals.
source: Western blot analysis performed on hippocampal extracts from both 3×Tg-AD and WT animals corroborates this result, showing a significantly lower expression of PSD-95 in 3×Tg-AD animals exposed to noise compared with not-exposed animals (Figure 6I and J; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.028).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 6I and J.

claim: The NOR test is a widely used behavioral paradigm for the assessment of object-recognition memory.
source: The NOR test is a widely used behavioral paradigm for the assessment of object-recognition memory, in which an animal has to discriminate a novel from an old object.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NOR test.

claim: Recognition memory depends on temporal lobe activity, specifically on the hippocampus.
source: Changes in the exploration time of the new and the old object are indicative of recognition memory, which depends on temporal lobe activity, specifically on the hippocampus (Ennaceur and De Souza Silva, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: At 3 M, 3×Tg-AD and WT mice exposed to noise did not exhibit any impairment in recognition memory compared to age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: We found that, at 3 M, 3×Tg-AD and WT mice exposed to noise did not exhibit any impairment in recognition memory compared to age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 7A and C; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by NOR test data shown in Figures 7A and C and Table 1.

claim: At 6 M, memory performance was significantly altered in 3×Tg-AD exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals, for both LTM and STM evaluations.
source: Interestingly, at 6 M memory performance was significantly altered in 3×Tg-AD exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals, for both LTM and STM evaluations (Figure 7B and D; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by NOR test data shown in Figures 7B and D and Table 1.

claim: No significant differences in recognition memory were found in WT animals exposed to noise compared to age-matched not-exposed mice at 6 M.
source: Consistent with functional and morphological evaluations, no significant differences in recognition memory were found in WT animals exposed to noise compared to age-matched not-exposed mice (Figure 7D; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by NOR test data shown in Figure 7D and Table 1.

claim: Differences in memory performance were independent of locomotor activity.
source: Finally, differences in memory performance were independent of locomotor activity, as we did not observe any differences between NE and NN mice in total distance traveled (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Memory deficits in 3×Tg AD mice reportedly manifest at about 8 months.
source: Given that memory deficits in 3×Tg AD mice reportedly manifest at about 8 months (Clinton et al., 2007; Stover et al., 2015; Cocco et al., 2020), our data suggest that hearing loss accelerates memory impairment in this transgenic mouse model of AD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on this mouse model.

claim: Hearing loss accelerates memory impairment in the 3×Tg AD transgenic mouse model.
source: Given that memory deficits in 3×Tg AD mice reportedly manifest at about 8 months (Clinton et al., 2007; Stover et al., 2015; Cocco et al., 2020), our data suggest that hearing loss accelerates memory impairment in this transgenic mouse model of AD.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the earlier appearance of memory deficits in noise-exposed AD mice.

claim: Simple linear regression analysis identified no relationship between ABR mean threshold and NOR performance in all experimental groups at 6 M.
source: Simple linear regression analysis across 6 M animals that underwent both ABR and NOR procedures (AD-NN n = 13; AD-NE n = 10; WT-NN n = 9; WT-NE n = 7) identified no relationship between ABR mean threshold and NOR performance in all experimental groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; AD-NN, r2 = 0.0049, p = 0.467; AD-NE, r2 = 0.0032, p = 0.878; WT-NN, r2 = 0.187, p = 0.244; WT-NE, r2 = 0.0009, p = 0.984).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: A significant statistical relationship was found between NOR performance and spine density in ACx in AD-NE mice at 6 M.
source: However, of note, we found in AD-NE (n = 4) a significant statistical relationship (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; r2 = 0.96, p = 0.019) between NOR and spine density data, suggesting that deficits in memory performance correlated with the central effects of hearing loss and altered structural plasticity of ACx circuitry.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deficits in memory performance correlated with the central effects of hearing loss and altered structural plasticity of ACx circuitry in AD-NE mice.
source: However, of note, we found in AD-NE (n = 4) a significant statistical relationship (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; r2 = 0.96, p = 0.019) between NOR and spine density data, suggesting that deficits in memory performance correlated with the central effects of hearing loss and altered structural plasticity of ACx circuitry.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between NOR performance and spine density.

claim: Sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure affects hippocampal synaptic function in 3×Tg-AD model.
source: Collectively, our results revealed that sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure affects hippocampal synaptic function, decreases spine density and accelerates memory deficits in 3×Tg-AD model.
evidence: This is a summary of the hippocampal findings from the study.

claim: Sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure decreases spine density in hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD model.
source: Collectively, our results revealed that sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure affects hippocampal synaptic function, decreases spine density and accelerates memory deficits in 3×Tg-AD model.
evidence: This is a summary of the morphological findings in hippocampus from the study.

claim: Sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure accelerates memory deficits in 3×Tg-AD model.
source: Collectively, our results revealed that sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure affects hippocampal synaptic function, decreases spine density and accelerates memory deficits in 3×Tg-AD model.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings from the study.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of tau is a well-known marker of neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Considering that hyperphosphorylation of tau is a well-known marker of neurodegenerative disorders and that tau phosphorylation is one of the earliest cytoskeletal changes in AD and a critical step in the formation of neurofibrillary tangles (Wischik et al., 1988), we evaluated tau phosphorylation at Ser396 (pTauSer396) which has been strongly linked to AD progression (Mondragón-Rodríguez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tau phosphorylation is one of the earliest cytoskeletal changes in AD and a critical step in the formation of neurofibrillary tangles.
source: Considering that hyperphosphorylation of tau is a well-known marker of neurodegenerative disorders and that tau phosphorylation is one of the earliest cytoskeletal changes in AD and a critical step in the formation of neurofibrillary tangles (Wischik et al., 1988), we evaluated tau phosphorylation at Ser396 (pTauSer396) which has been strongly linked to AD progression (Mondragón-Rodríguez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Tau phosphorylation at Ser396 has been strongly linked to AD progression.
source: Considering that hyperphosphorylation of tau is a well-known marker of neurodegenerative disorders and that tau phosphorylation is one of the earliest cytoskeletal changes in AD and a critical step in the formation of neurofibrillary tangles (Wischik et al., 1988), we evaluated tau phosphorylation at Ser396 (pTauSer396) which has been strongly linked to AD progression (Mondragón-Rodríguez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mondragón-Rodríguez et al., 2014.

claim: Western blot analysis showed a marked increase of pTauSer396 in hippocampi of 6 M transgenic mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: Our Western blot analysis performed on the hippocampi of 3×Tg-AD and WT mice showed a marked increase of pTauSer396 in 6 M transgenic mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 8A and B; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN, p = 0.006), whereas no significant differences were observed between WT-NE and WT-NN groups (Figure 8A and B; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, WT-NE vs. WT-NN mice p = 0.49).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 8A and B.

claim: No significant differences in pTauSer396 were observed between WT-NE and WT-NN groups at 6 M.
source: Our Western blot analysis performed on the hippocampi of 3×Tg-AD and WT mice showed a marked increase of pTauSer396 in 6 M transgenic mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 8A and B; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN, p = 0.006), whereas no significant differences were observed between WT-NE and WT-NN groups (Figure 8A and B; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, WT-NE vs. WT-NN mice p = 0.49).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 8A and B.

claim: TNF-α and IL-1β are well-known inflammatory markers playing a key role in neurodegenerative disease.
source: We also studied TNF-α and IL-1β, which are well-known inflammatory markers playing a key role in neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these inflammatory markers.

claim: Western blot and ELISA analyses showed significant increases of both TNF-α (~90%) and IL-1β in the hippocampus of 6 M 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: Data of Western blot and ELISA analyses showed significant increases of both TNF-α (~90%) and IL-1β (7.50 ± 1.58 vs. 2.88 ± 0.47 pg/mg) in the hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 8C–E) and no differences between WT-NN vs. WT-NE mice (Figure 8C–E; TNF-α, n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.015; IL-1β, n = 3 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figures 8C-E.

claim: No differences in TNF-α and IL-1β were found between WT-NN vs. WT-NE mice at 6 M.
source: Data of Western blot and ELISA analyses showed significant increases of both TNF-α (~90%) and IL-1β (7.50 ± 1.58 vs. 2.88 ± 0.47 pg/mg) in the hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise compared with age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 8C–E) and no differences between WT-NN vs. WT-NE mice (Figure 8C–E; TNF-α, n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.015; IL-1β, n = 3 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figures 8C-E.

claim: Redox imbalance is a well-known consequence of noise-induced hearing loss.
source: To further characterize molecular underpinnings of hippocampal dysfunctions, we investigated oxidative stress, considering that redox imbalance is a well-known consequence of noise-induced hearing loss (Fetoni et al., 2019) and hippocampus is particularly prone to hearing loss-related oxidative stress (Stebbings et al., 2016; Nadhimi and Llano, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hippocampus is particularly prone to hearing loss-related oxidative stress.
source: To further characterize molecular underpinnings of hippocampal dysfunctions, we investigated oxidative stress, considering that redox imbalance is a well-known consequence of noise-induced hearing loss (Fetoni et al., 2019) and hippocampus is particularly prone to hearing loss-related oxidative stress (Stebbings et al., 2016; Nadhimi and Llano, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Immunofluorescence analyses showed an increase of ROS in DG and CA1 regions of the hippocampus of 6 M transgenic mice exposed to noise, compared with age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses performed by using dihydroethidium (DHE) assay in coronal sections of both 6 M AD and WT mice showed an increase of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in DG (Figure 9C–D, I) and CA1 (Figure 9G–H, I) regions of the hippocampus of transgenic mice exposed to noise, compared with age-matched not-exposed animals.
evidence: This is supported by DHE immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Fluorescence signal quantification showed a significant increase of fluorescence intensity specifically in AD-NE compared with AD-NN mice in hippocampal CA1 and DG regions.
source: Fluorescence signal quantification showed a significant increase of fluorescence intensity specifically in AD-NE compared with AD-NN mice (Figure 9I and J; n = 3 animals/group; Student's t-test, CA1, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.001; DG AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.008).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of DHE fluorescence shown in Figures 9I and J.

claim: Increased ROS production can lead to lipid peroxidation.
source: Furthermore, considering that increased ROS production can lead to lipid peroxidation (Angelova and Abramov, 2018), we assessed lipid peroxidative damage.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Peroxidation of the membrane lipid bilayer is one of the major sources of free radical-mediated injury that directly damages neurons.
source: Peroxidation of the membrane lipid bilayer is one of the major sources of free radical-mediated injury that directly damages neurons causing increased membrane rigidity, decreased activity of membrane-bound enzymes, impairment of membrane receptors, and altered membrane permeability eventually leading to cell death (Tekpli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: An increase of 4-HNE was found in the hippocampus of 6 M 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise, compared to age-matched not-exposed mice.
source: Of note, our results revealed an increase of 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), a key marker of lipid peroxidation, in the hippocampus of 6 M 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise, compared to age-matched not-exposed mice (Figure 10C–D and G–H).
evidence: This is supported by 4-HNE immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The increase in 4-HNE was significant in both CA1 and DG hippocampal regions of 6 M AD-NE mice compared to AD-NN mice.
source: This difference was significant in both CA1 and DG hippocampal regions, as confirmed by quantitative fluorescence signal analysis (Figure 10I and J; n = 3 animals/group; Student's t-test, CA1, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.002; DG, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of 4-HNE fluorescence shown in Figures 10I and J.

claim: No significant changes in 4-HNE were found in WT-NE vs. WT-NN mice at 6 M.
source: No significant changes were found in WT-NE vs. WT-NN mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text following the 4-HNE analysis.

claim: Dot blot analysis showed an increase of NT formation in hippocampal samples of 6 M AD-NE mice, compared to age-matched AD-NN animals.
source: Dot blot analysis showed an increase of NT formation in hippocampal samples of 6 M AD-NE mice, compared to age-matched AD-NN animals (Figure 10—figure supplement 1; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN, p = 0.038).
evidence: This is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protein tyrosine nitration represents a prominent post-translational redox modification and it is associated with different diseases.
source: Indeed, protein tyrosine nitration represents a prominent post-translational redox modification and it is associated with different diseases (Ischiropoulos and Beckman, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a significant increase of the pro-apoptotic Bax in hippocampi of 6 M AD-NE mice compared to age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: Western bot analysis revealed a significant increase of the pro-apoptotic Bax (n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.004) and active Caspase-3 (n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.024) proteins in hippocampi of AD-NE mice compared to age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a significant increase of active Caspase-3 in hippocampi of 6 M AD-NE mice compared to age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: Western bot analysis revealed a significant increase of the pro-apoptotic Bax (n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.004) and active Caspase-3 (n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.024) proteins in hippocampi of AD-NE mice compared to age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed no changes in SOD2 expression in the hippocampus of noise-exposed animals compared to not-exposed groups, neither in 3×Tg AD nor in WT mice at 6 M.
source: Our Western blot analysis revealed no changes in SOD2 expression in the hippocampus of noise-exposed animals compared to not-exposed groups, neither in 3×Tg AD nor in WT mice at 6 M (Figure 11A and B; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, WT-NE vs. WT-NN mice, p = 0.81; AD-NE vs. AD-NN mice, p = 0.76).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 11A and B.

claim: WT-NE mice showed increased HO-1 expression compared to WT-NN animals at 6 M.
source: WT-NE mice showed increased HO-1 expression compared to WT-NN animals (Figure 11C and D; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, p = 0.006), suggesting an endogenous antioxidant response activation to face a toxic insult.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 11C and D.

claim: Increased HO-1 expression in WT-NE mice suggests an endogenous antioxidant response activation to face a toxic insult.
source: WT-NE mice showed increased HO-1 expression compared to WT-NN animals (Figure 11C and D; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, p = 0.006), suggesting an endogenous antioxidant response activation to face a toxic insult.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HO-1 upregulation in WT-NE mice.

claim: No significant modulation of HO-1 expression was found in the hippocampus of 6 M 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise, compared to age-matched not-exposed animals.
source: Conversely, no significant modulation of HO-1 expression was found in the hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise, compared to age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 11C and D; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, p = 0.93), likely due to an impaired ability of the endogenous antioxidant response to counteract oxidative stress and to restore redox balance.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 11C and D.

claim: The lack of HO-1 upregulation in AD-NE mice is likely due to an impaired ability of the endogenous antioxidant response to counteract oxidative stress and to restore redox balance.
source: Conversely, no significant modulation of HO-1 expression was found in the hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice exposed to noise, compared to age-matched not-exposed animals (Figure 11C and D; n = 4 animals/group; Student's t-test, p = 0.93), likely due to an impaired ability of the endogenous antioxidant response to counteract oxidative stress and to restore redox balance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lack of HO-1 response in AD-NE mice.

claim: Hearing impairment is known as a major clinical risk factor for cognitive decline.
source: Hearing impairment is known as a major clinical risk factor for cognitive decline (Gates and Mills, 2005; Lin et al., 2011; Loughrey et al., 2018; Griffiths et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2021), with relevant clinical implications for dementia prevention, diagnosis, and treatment (Dawes et al., 2015; Taljaard et al., 2016; Livingston et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The complex pathophysiological relation between hearing impairment and dementia remains to be fully defined.
source: However, the complex pathophysiological relation between hearing impairment and dementia remains to be fully defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Auditory sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure in young mice caused structural and functional changes in ACx.
source: The present research shows that auditory sensory deprivation induced by noise exposure in young mice (i.e., at 2 M, when AD phenotype is not manifested yet in 3×Tg AD mice) caused structural and functional changes in ACx.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on ACx changes.

claim: WT animals recovered over time from noise-induced changes in ACx.
source: Notably, WT animals recovered over time, whereas 3×Tg-AD mice failed to rescue central damage associated with hearing loss, showing not only persistent synaptic and morphological alterations in the ACx, but also hippocampal dysfunction, increased tau phosphorylation, and anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of AD phenotype observed in age-matched 3×Tg-AD mice not exposed to noise.
evidence: This is a summary of the differential recovery between WT and AD mice.

claim: 3×Tg-AD mice failed to rescue central damage associated with hearing loss.
source: Notably, WT animals recovered over time, whereas 3×Tg-AD mice failed to rescue central damage associated with hearing loss, showing not only persistent synaptic and morphological alterations in the ACx, but also hippocampal dysfunction, increased tau phosphorylation, and anticipated memory deficits compared to the expected time-course of AD phenotype observed in age-matched 3×Tg-AD mice not exposed to noise.
evidence: This is a summary of the persistent alterations in AD mice.

claim: Neuroinflammation and redox imbalance were found in hippocampi of 6 M AD-NE mice.
source: Neuroinflammation and redox imbalance were found in hippocampi of 6 M AD-NE mice that might be related to the reduced ability of the central structures to rescue noise-induced detrimental effects, making this experimental model of AD more vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss.
evidence: This is a summary of the molecular findings in hippocampus.

claim: Neuroinflammation and redox imbalance might be related to the reduced ability of the central structures to rescue noise-induced detrimental effects in AD mice.
source: Neuroinflammation and redox imbalance were found in hippocampi of 6 M AD-NE mice that might be related to the reduced ability of the central structures to rescue noise-induced detrimental effects, making this experimental model of AD more vulnerable to central damage induced by hearing loss.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between molecular changes and vulnerability.

claim: No differences in baseline auditory thresholds were found between AD-NN and WT-NN animals at 3 and 6 M.
source: In our study, no differences in baseline auditory thresholds were found between AD-NN and WT-NN animals at 3 and 6 M, consistent with previous data reporting alterations in cochlear functions starting from 9 M in other models of AD pathology (Wang and Wu, 2015; O'Leary et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by ABR measurements and consistent with previous studies.

claim: Alterations in cochlear functions start from 9 M in other models of AD pathology.
source: In our study, no differences in baseline auditory thresholds were found between AD-NN and WT-NN animals at 3 and 6 M, consistent with previous data reporting alterations in cochlear functions starting from 9 M in other models of AD pathology (Wang and Wu, 2015; O'Leary et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The acoustic trauma caused permanent increase of auditory threshold of about 30–40 dB, spanning at all frequencies analyzed in both strains.
source: The acoustic trauma caused permanent increase of auditory threshold of about 30–40 dB, spanning at all frequencies analyzed in both strains, estimated 1 and 4 months after the onset of trauma sessions (corresponding to 3 and 6 M of mouse age), indicating no differences in cochlear susceptibility to noise exposure between WT and 3×Tg-AD animals.
evidence: This is a summary of the ABR threshold data.

claim: There are no differences in cochlear susceptibility to noise exposure between WT and 3×Tg-AD animals.
source: The acoustic trauma caused permanent increase of auditory threshold of about 30–40 dB, spanning at all frequencies analyzed in both strains, estimated 1 and 4 months after the onset of trauma sessions (corresponding to 3 and 6 M of mouse age), indicating no differences in cochlear susceptibility to noise exposure between WT and 3×Tg-AD animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the similar threshold increases in both strains.

claim: The spine loss observed in 3 M animals might be caused by deafferentation and activity-dependent remodeling of neuronal connectivity.
source: The spine loss observed in 3 M animals might be caused by deafferentation and activity-dependent remodeling of neuronal connectivity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the spine loss mechanism.

claim: Noise-induced morphological changes in ACx were accompanied with decreased excitatory synaptic responses of neurons within layer II/III.
source: Accordingly, our electrophysiological analyses on ACx brain slices revealed that noise-induced morphological changes were accompanied with decreased excitatory synaptic responses of neurons within layer II/III.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from the study.

claim: Central auditory processing dysfunction is highly evident in patients with AD.
source: Our results showing a high vulnerability of auditory central structures to sensory deprivation in a transgenic model of AD are consistent with clinical evidence. Indeed, central auditory processing dysfunction is highly evident in patients with AD (Idrizbegovic et al., 2011), and pathological changes have also been found in the ascending auditory pathway (Sinha et al., 1993; Parvizi et al., 2001; Baloyannis et al., 2009) as well as in the ACx (Lewis et al., 1987; Baloyannis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical research.

claim: Pathological changes have been found in the ascending auditory pathway in AD patients.
source: Our results showing a high vulnerability of auditory central structures to sensory deprivation in a transgenic model of AD are consistent with clinical evidence. Indeed, central auditory processing dysfunction is highly evident in patients with AD (Idrizbegovic et al., 2011), and pathological changes have also been found in the ascending auditory pathway (Sinha et al., 1993; Parvizi et al., 2001; Baloyannis et al., 2009) as well as in the ACx (Lewis et al., 1987; Baloyannis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Pathological changes have been found in the ACx in AD patients.
source: Our results showing a high vulnerability of auditory central structures to sensory deprivation in a transgenic model of AD are consistent with clinical evidence. Indeed, central auditory processing dysfunction is highly evident in patients with AD (Idrizbegovic et al., 2011), and pathological changes have also been found in the ascending auditory pathway (Sinha et al., 1993; Parvizi et al., 2001; Baloyannis et al., 2009) as well as in the ACx (Lewis et al., 1987; Baloyannis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Hippocampus participates in processing of auditory information conveyed by the lemniscal and non-lemniscal paths.
source: It is known that hippocampus participates in processing of auditory information conveyed by the lemniscal and non-lemniscal paths (Steward, 1976; Germroth et al., 1989; Moxon et al., 1999; Budinger and Scheich, 2009; Munoz-Lopez et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both lemniscal and non-lemniscal pathways convey information from the cochlear nuclei to the hippocampus.
source: Both of these pathways convey information from the cochlear nuclei to the hippocampus, which is critically involved in spatial learning tasks (Adams et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The hippocampus is critically involved in spatial learning tasks.
source: Both of these pathways convey information from the cochlear nuclei to the hippocampus, which is critically involved in spatial learning tasks (Adams et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The hippocampus can respond to acoustic as well as to visual and olfactory stimuli as it processes such information to create spatial memories.
source: On the other hand, the hippocampus can respond to acoustic as well as to visual and olfactory stimuli as it processes such information to create spatial memories (Kemp and Manahan-Vaughan, 2008; André and Manahan-Vaughan, 2013; Dietz and Manahan-Vaughan, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Age-related hearing loss in an animal model of presbycusis is accompanied by extensive reorganization of plasticity-related neurotransmitter expression in ACx and hippocampus.
source: Moreover, it has been reported that age-related hearing loss in an animal model of presbycusis is accompanied by extensive reorganization of plasticity-related neurotransmitter expression in ACx and hippocampus, and is associated with altered hippocampal synaptic plasticity, as well as memory impairments (Beckmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Age-related hearing loss is associated with altered hippocampal synaptic plasticity and memory impairments.
source: Moreover, it has been reported that age-related hearing loss in an animal model of presbycusis is accompanied by extensive reorganization of plasticity-related neurotransmitter expression in ACx and hippocampus, and is associated with altered hippocampal synaptic plasticity, as well as memory impairments (Beckmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The majority of studies indicate that 7–9 months is the time-window when cognitive deficits most often manifest in 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: Although a certain degree of heterogeneity has been reported in 3×Tg-AD mouse model regarding the onset and progression of cognitive deficits, the majority of studies including ours indicate that 7–9 months is the time-window when cognitive deficits most often manifest (Clinton et al., 2007; Martinez-Coria et al., 2010; Chakroborty et al., 2019; Joseph et al., 2019; Cocco et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies including the authors' own work.

claim: Memory performance in 6 M 3×Tg-AD mice was comparable to that of WT mice.
source: Consistently, memory performance in 6 M 3×Tg-AD mice was comparable to that of WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by the NOR test data presented in the study.

claim: Sensory deprivation induced by noise accelerated cognitive decline in 3×Tg-AD mice, anticipating it at 6 M of age.
source: Of note, our study showed that sensory deprivation induced by noise accelerated cognitive decline in 3×Tg-AD mice, anticipating it at 6 M of age, as revealed by decreased LTM and STM recognition memory performance in NOR test.
evidence: This is supported by the NOR test data showing earlier memory deficits in noise-exposed AD mice.

claim: The interplay between oxidative stress and neuroinflammation is a common feature of AD pathology.
source: The interplay between oxidative stress and neuroinflammation is a common feature of AD pathology and production of oxidizing free radicals, including ROS and reactive nitrogen species, can be induced by increased cytokine production (Naik and Dixit, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Production of oxidizing free radicals can be induced by increased cytokine production.
source: The interplay between oxidative stress and neuroinflammation is a common feature of AD pathology and production of oxidizing free radicals, including ROS and reactive nitrogen species, can be induced by increased cytokine production (Naik and Dixit, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Oxidative stress leads to increased tau phosphorylation in vitro.
source: Moreover, several studies also showed that oxidative stress leads to increased tau phosphorylation in vitro (Zhu et al., 2005; Su et al., 2010) and peroxidative damage and 4-HNE expression facilitated aggregation of phosphorylated tau (Pérez et al., 2000), inducing tau hyperphosphorylation (Gómez-Ramos et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Peroxidative damage and 4-HNE expression facilitated aggregation of phosphorylated tau.
source: Moreover, several studies also showed that oxidative stress leads to increased tau phosphorylation in vitro (Zhu et al., 2005; Su et al., 2010) and peroxidative damage and 4-HNE expression facilitated aggregation of phosphorylated tau (Pérez et al., 2000), inducing tau hyperphosphorylation (Gómez-Ramos et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hyperphosphorylated tau accumulation in the hippocampus and neocortex and cognitive impairment have been observed as a consequence of chronic noise exposure.
source: Moreover, hyperphosphorylated tau accumulation in the hippocampus and neocortex and cognitive impairment have been observed as a consequence of chronic noise exposure in previous studies (Cui et al., 2012; Park et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Auditory sensory deprivation can exacerbate pathological molecular pathways of AD, accelerating cognitive decline.
source: Our findings suggest that auditory sensory deprivation can exacerbate pathological molecular pathways of AD, accelerating cognitive decline.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings on molecular and behavioral changes.

claim: HO can interact with APP family members resulting in HO inhibition.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with previous studies demonstrating that HO can interact with APP family members resulting in HO inhibition. Accordingly, in APP mutant mice HO-1 as well as bilirubin levels were significantly decreased while oxidative stress-induced neurotoxicity was markedly increased (Takahashi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In APP mutant mice HO-1 as well as bilirubin levels were significantly decreased while oxidative stress-induced neurotoxicity was markedly increased.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with previous studies demonstrating that HO can interact with APP family members resulting in HO inhibition. Accordingly, in APP mutant mice HO-1 as well as bilirubin levels were significantly decreased while oxidative stress-induced neurotoxicity was markedly increased (Takahashi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Oxidative stress is involved in various pathological states including several age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
